name: Jaw surgery (orthognathic)

lead: Orthognathic surgery repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw, chin or all three. In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as the major structural option for a recessed jaw, facial balance, profile and a straighter bite and smile; medically it is used for underbites, overbites, open bites, asymmetry, jaw-joint problems and sleep apnoea.

Surgeons cut the jawbones from inside the mouth, move them to a planned position and fix them with titanium plates and screws, usually after orthodontic preparation. Procedures include Le Fort I for the upper jaw, sagittal split for the lower jaw and genioplasty for the chin, sometimes combined as two-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery. Virtual 3D planning and custom splints are increasingly used. Medical literature documents functional outcomes well and is more limited on purely cosmetic goals.

paras: People typically go through orthodontics first, often braces, then surgery planned with a surgeon and orthodontist, followed by recovery over weeks to months. Forum discussion centers on surgeon choice, insurance, braces timing and recovery.

Reviews describe bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, jaw-joint effects, relapse and hardware problems, with recovery lasting weeks to months. A systematic review estimated body dysmorphic disorder is more common among orthognathic surgery patients than in the general community.

angle.text: Orthognathic surgery cuts and repositions the upper jaw, lower jaw and chin, realigning the bite and midface for better facial balance and profile. The change in jaw position is itself the visible result, though reports note functional gains and cosmetic outcomes do not always match.

lead: Orthognathic surgery, also called corrective jaw surgery, reshapes the jaws and lower face to treat structural, growth, airway, jaw-joint and bite problems, and can also be used for facial balance and symmetry.[1] The operation is usually done through the mouth: bone is cut, moved and fixed in a new position, and it is typically coordinated with orthodontic treatment.[1][2]

Main procedures include the Le Fort I osteotomy for the upper jaw, the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy for the lower jaw, and genioplasty for the chin; surgeons may combine them in two-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery.[1][3] Reviews describe expanding indications for upper-airway obstruction, computer-assisted planning, patient-specific fixation and shifts in the orthodontic-surgical sequence over the past two decades.[4]

In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as one of the most consequential procedures, discussed alongside implants, rhinoplasty and orthodontics, with extensive talk about risk and surgeon choice.[5][6][7]

paras: The Le Fort I osteotomy moves the maxilla and is described in dedicated reviews that cover indications, contraindications, preoperative assessment, technique and complications.[8] The bilateral sagittal split osteotomy moves the lower jaw forward or back, and genioplasty repositions the chin and may be used alone or alongside jaw surgery.[1][2]

Genioplasty is described as an essential component when the chin position affects lower-face aesthetics, and contemporary reviews cover techniques, stability, fixation and complications.[2] Asymmetry cases are described as challenging, with 3D diagnosis and virtual planning increasingly helpful.[9]

A surgical team usually includes surgeons and orthodontists, with X-rays, photographs and 3D software used to predict the result and to help patients understand the plan.[1] Presurgical orthodontics has traditionally taken up to a year, with surgery-first approaches and clear aligners as newer alternatives.[1]

A systematic review of 12 studies found virtual planning accurate to under 2 mm on average in the maxilla and mandible in three planes, and a prospective multicentre study of 65 patients evaluated a computer-aided surgical simulation protocol against actual outcomes.[10] A randomised trial compared periodontal health and quality of life with clear aligners versus fixed appliances after orthognathic surgery.[11]

Human research on orthognathic surgery covers planning accuracy, stability, complications, patient outcomes and sleep apnoea. A hierarchy-of-stability update reported that stability differs among surgical movements, with correction of asymmetry and chin repositioning very stable under rigid fixation.[12] A review of 655 patients examined the incidence of complications and problems after orthognathic surgery.[13] A 2016 individual-patient meta-analysis examined criteria associated with outcomes of maxillomandibular advancement for sleep apnoea.[14]

A systematic review found a weighted prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder of 11.2 percent in orthognathic surgery settings, compared with 1.9 percent in the adult community, and noted that the condition is poorly identified in practice.[15] Randomised trials have compared post-surgical orthodontic methods and maxilla-guided versus mandible-guided approaches with patient-specific implants.[11][16]

Wikipedia lists bleeding, swelling, infection, nausea and nerve-related numbness as the main risks, with the numbness usually temporary but occasionally permanent.[1] Initial healing is described as taking about two to six weeks, with complete bone healing taking longer.[1]

A forum member's long post summarising complications reported on forums and social media lists nerve damage, persistent numbness and altered sensation among the issues patients describe; another member who had a double-jaw operation for sleep apnoea reported good functional results but an unsatisfactory aesthetic outcome and later bone contouring.[7][6]

Forum threads describe jaw surgery as a major step for people with a recessed jaw, discussing whether to have a bimaxillary or single-jaw operation, when to start orthodontics and how age affects eligibility.[5] Members also discuss surgery abroad, recovery and complications, and compare jaw surgery with implants and other procedures.[6][7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org jaw surgery appears in threads on planning, braces, surgeon selection, recovery and complications, from first-time patients to people reporting revisions.[5][6][7]

claims.claim: Bimax or a single-jaw operation can fix a recessed jaw, and the result is often better than a jaw-jut test suggests.
Jaw surgery carries serious risks that are underreported, including permanent numbness.
Jaw surgery can improve function but disappoint cosmetically.
Getting insurance to cover jaw surgery depends on proving a functional problem.

timeline.event: Simon P. Hullihen publishes one of the first known orthognathic cases.[1]
Hugo Obwegeser and Trauner are credited with the bilateral sagittal split osteotomy, according to an AI-generated encyclopedia overview.[3]
Rigid titanium plate fixation reduces the need for long jaw immobilisation.[3]
Raffaini introduces lower-jaw surgery under local anaesthesia with sedation, shortening hospital stay.[1]
An updated hierarchy of stability for orthognathic procedures with rigid fixation is published.[12]
A prospective multicentre study evaluates computer-aided surgical simulation accuracy.[10]
